prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is one of the cleanest cases on the shortlist of a sharp theoretical prediction followed by an unexpected experimental discovery. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle in 2011, and in 2018 Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. The discovery is at the centre of the case, and it has produced a new, tunable platform for strongly correlated and topological matter that many groups now use. It is also the only candidate that all seven members who ranked it placed in their top seven, which suggests broad if not enthusiastic support. The theory-plus-experiment trio maps onto the three names without forcing.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated phases are still debated, and results depend strongly on twist-angle disorder and sample quality. Cao, Fatemi and other first authors, and the Dean, Young, Efetov, Kim and Yazdani groups, are outside the credited names. A prize now could look early compared with B022 and B045, which are more mature and have clearer priority histories.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B045 first as a mature, overdue topological-insulator case with a compact Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio, and he ranked B030 second while warning that the unsettled pairing mechanism may argue for waiting.
responses.response: I take the maturity warning seriously, but I would separate the discovery from the mechanism. The flat band origin of the correlated insulators is stable and has been reproduced widely and extended to other moire systems. An unsettled pairing mechanism did not stop earlier prizes for high-temperature superconductivity or the quantum Hall effects. I agree that B045 is the more mature case. My difficulty is attribution, since Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum well and Zhang is deceased, so any three-person split leaves a hole in the credit story that the B030 trio does not.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first, calling the Katori-Ye pairing clean and timely, and ranked B004 second as a natural successor to the 2016 topological prize.
responses.response: I agree that B022 has the cleanest attribution of any entry. My reservation is whether a ten to eighteen digit improvement in an established measurement is a discovery in the sense that the centre of the case should be a discovery. The clock enables discoveries, such as redshift tests and constants searches, but those have not yet happened. I would not block B022, and I hold it as my first alternative. On B004, I would not give a second topological prize this soon after 2016 and then split the topological credit between B004 and B045. The quantum anomalous Hall step is a later and distinct achievement.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B030 only seventh, arguing that the interpretation of the correlated states is not yet stable and recognition may be somewhat early; he also disclosed a possible bias on circuit QED.
responses.response: I think this is the strongest objection to my first choice, and I am not dismissing it. The distinction I would draw is that the prediction was specific and quantitative and the experiment confirmed it in a way that nobody expected, even if the full theory of the phases is unfinished. I note that Johansson's own rank-two choice, B039, runs into the 2025 circuit prize, and he has flagged his own proximity to it. That does not make B039 wrong, but I would give weight to the argument that two quantum-circuit prizes in consecutive years would look repetitive.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked B022 first and B002 second, and argued that baryon acoustic oscillations are a clear, mature standard-ruler discovery, though credit for the theory precursors is outside the credited names.
responses.response: BAO is directly relevant to the dark-energy questions I care about, which is why I ranked it fifth. My problem is the same as yours. Two large survey collaborations made the 2005 detections, and the theoretical origin in Peebles-Yu and Sunyaev-Zeldovich sits outside the credited set, so a three-person prize misrepresents both the observation and the idea. Recent DESI hints of evolving dark energy also make the physical meaning in flux, even if the measurement is not. I would keep B002 below the condensed-matter and precision-measurement cases for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept a prize at about eight years after the experimental discovery while the pairing mechanism remains unsettled.
Whether Cao and Fatemi and the other experimental groups can be fairly omitted under the three-person limit.
Whether the strong first-place support for B022 should outweigh the stronger cross-member breadth for B030.
How to handle the topological-insulator credit, in B045 and B004, if the committee instead prefers that area.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none of them appears among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate.
